title: What Does It Mean to Be a Disciple of Jesus?
subtitle: Jesus did not call converts. He called disciples, apprentices who learn to live his life. What Scripture, church history, and honest research say about how a person is actually changed, why so many believers stall, and the slow work of becoming like the one you follow.

parts.title: Saved and Stuck
parts.body:
You believe. You are not in doubt about the gospel, not really. You crossed the line of faith years ago, you go to church, you would tell anyone who asked that Jesus is Lord and mean it. And yet if you are honest, you are stuck. The person you are today is not noticeably different from the person you were five years ago. The same temper, the same anxieties, the same private habits you have confessed a hundred times and never quite left. You are saved and you are stalled, and no one talks about the second part.

It is a strange ache, because nothing is obviously wrong. You are not in scandal. You are not deconstructing. You are just plateaued, running a Christian life that has become a set of activities, church on Sunday, a podcast in the car, a prayer when the bottom drops out, and underneath it a quiet suspicion that this is not what Jesus had in mind. You hear about people whose lives were genuinely changed and you wonder why yours has not been, and you assume the problem is that you are not trying hard enough, or not feeling enough, or not enough.

Maybe you have tried to fix it the way the church taught you, with more information. Another study, another book, another conference, more truth poured into a life that already knew more than it was living. And the gap between what you know and who you are only widened, until you started to feel like a hypocrite for knowing so much and changing so little. That gap, between the believer's knowledge and the believer's life, is the great unaddressed crisis of the modern church, and you are standing in it.

Here is what no one told you. The reason you are stuck is not that you lack information or sincerity. It is that somewhere along the way you were handed a Christianity with the discipleship taken out, a gospel that offered forgiveness without apprenticeship, a ticket to heaven with no school for becoming like Jesus along the way. You were made a believer and never quite made a disciple, and the two are not the same. Jesus never asked anyone to believe in him and stop there. He said follow me, which is the beginning of a long and ordinary apprenticeship that the church forgot to mention.

parts.title: What Is at Stake in a Stalled Faith
parts.body:
The stakes are not first about heaven. They are about whether the Christian life is real. Jesus said you will know a tree by its fruit, and a faith that produces no growing likeness to Christ over years raises a question the church is afraid to ask out loud, whether it was ever a living faith or only an assent. This is not said to terrify the struggling believer, who is precisely the one taking the question seriously. It is said because a Christianity that has quietly given up on actual change has given up on the very thing Jesus came to do, which was not only to forgive sinners but to make them new.

The stakes are also corporate, because stalled disciples make a powerless church. A congregation full of people who believe correctly and live indistinguishably from their neighbors has nothing to offer a watching world but more religion, and the world has plenty of that. The early church turned an empire upside down not because its members held the right opinions but because they had visibly become a different kind of people, who forgave their enemies, shared their goods, and went to their deaths singing. The world was converted by disciples, not by believers, and it always has been.

And the stakes are personal in a way that the language of getting saved obscures. You were made for more than a managed sinfulness and a deferred heaven. You were made to be transformed, conformed to the image of the Son, to become in actual fact a person who loves the way he loves, who is unhurried and unafraid and free. That transformation is the inheritance Christ died to give you, and to settle for a forgiven stagnation is to leave most of the gift in the box. The skeptic, watching, concludes that Christianity changes nothing because he keeps meeting Christians it has not changed, and the tragedy is not only his unbelief but their unclaimed inheritance.

parts.title: What Scripture Actually Means by Disciple
parts.body:
Recover the word itself, because we have lost it. A disciple, in the world of the New Testament, was an apprentice, a person who attached themselves to a teacher in order to learn not merely his ideas but his whole way of life. A disciple followed a rabbi everywhere, ate what he ate, watched how he handled money and anger and interruption, and slowly became like him. The goal of a disciple, Jesus said, is to become like his teacher. Discipleship was never primarily a transfer of information. It was an apprenticeship of the whole life to a master, and the master Jesus calls us to apprentice ourselves to is himself.

So when Jesus calls, he does not say believe the following propositions. He says follow me, the same words a rabbi used to recruit an apprentice, and the men who heard them left their nets and their tables and reorganized their entire lives around being with him. That is the first and most forgotten thing about discipleship, that it is being with Jesus before it is doing anything for him. He appointed the twelve, Mark says, so that they might be with him, and only then that he might send them out. The being with comes first, and the becoming like flows out of it, and the doing for follows from both. We have inverted the order, demanding activity from people who have never learned to simply be with him, and wondering why they burn out unchanged.

Jesus was also relentlessly honest that this apprenticeship costs everything, which the modern invitation hides. Count the cost, he said, like a man building a tower or a king going to war, because whoever does not take up his cross and follow is not able to be my disciple. He turned away the eager and the half-hearted with a bluntness that would get a pastor fired today, because he was not recruiting admirers but apprentices, and an apprentice gives the master his whole life or he is not really one. The gospel is free, but the following is total, and a discipleship that costs nothing forms no one.

And Jesus told us exactly how the transformation happens, in the image of the vine. Abide in me, he said, and I in you, for apart from me you can do nothing. The branch does not produce grapes by trying harder. It produces them by staying connected to the vine, drawing its life from a source outside itself, and the fruit comes as the natural overflow of the connection. This is the great secret the stalled believer needs. You do not change yourself by gritting your teeth at your sins. You change by abiding, by staying so connected to Christ through the ordinary means he gave, his Word, his table, his Spirit, his people, prayer, that his life flows into you and slowly bears its fruit. The disciplines of grace are not how you earn change. They are how you stay near the vine while he produces it.

Then comes the commission, which defines the church's whole task in one sentence and corrects a generation of evangelism. Go and make disciples, Jesus said, not go and make converts, baptizing them and teaching them to obey everything I have commanded. The aim was never a decision but an apprentice, a person being taught over time to actually obey, to live the life. The church that counts conversions and never makes disciples has not done a smaller version of the commission. It has done a different thing, and the difference is the difference between a maternity ward that delivers babies and walks away, and a family that raises them. Jesus commanded the family, and we have too often settled for the ward.

parts.title: How the Church Has Made Disciples
parts.body:
The early church took the making of disciples with a seriousness that shames our hurry. Before a convert was baptized, they passed through the catechumenate, a period of formation that often lasted two or three years, in which they were taught the faith, formed in its practices, and watched to see whether their lives were actually changing, before they were ever admitted to the table. The church assumed that becoming a Christian was a slow apprenticeship, not a single decision, and it built a long on-ramp to match. We have kept the decision and demolished the on-ramp, and then we wonder at the shallowness of the result.

When the empire became nominally Christian and the cost of faith collapsed, the radical impulse fled to the desert. The monastic movement was, at its root, a discipleship movement, an attempt to take Jesus seriously when the wider church had grown comfortable. Benedict wrote a Rule, a structured way of life ordering prayer, work, study, and community around the goal of being formed into Christ, and his genius was the recognition that transformation happens through a rhythm of practices sustained over years, not through bursts of inspiration. The Rule assumed what we forget, that you become what you repeatedly do in the presence of God.

The insight kept resurfacing whenever the church grew formal and cold. The medieval friars, the devotio moderna that produced the Imitation of Christ, the Puritans with their rigorous self-examination and their conviction that godliness was a discipline to be practiced, all were recoveries of the same buried truth, that a disciple is made by intentional formation and not by accident. None of them imagined that a person drifts into Christlikeness. They built structures to pursue it on purpose.

Nowhere is this clearer than in the early Methodist movement, which is in many ways a master class in discipleship for the modern church to relearn. John Wesley did not merely preach for decisions. He gathered every convert into a small group he called a class and a smaller, more searching one he called a band, where ordinary people met weekly to answer the question, how is it with your soul, to confess sin, to watch over one another in love, and to hold each other to a way of life. The genius was structural. Wesley knew that the fire of a revival meeting would die in a week without a vessel to carry it, and the class meeting was the vessel. The movement that resulted changed a nation, not because Wesley had a better message than others, but because he had a better method of forming disciples, and the church has been forgetting and rediscovering his lesson ever since.

parts.title: Knowledge Tested Against Scripture
parts.body: Discipleship is the question of how a human being is actually changed, and on that question honest researchers have learned a great deal that a believer can receive gratefully and critically at once, because all truth is God's truth. What follows takes five bodies of secular insight on formation and change seriously, names what each sees clearly, and tests each against Scripture, because every theory of how people change carries a hidden picture of what a person is, and the picture is where the wisdom is won or lost.

secular.author: Charles Duhigg and behavioral research
secular.whatItGetsRight: Duhigg and the literature on habit show that most of life runs on automatic routines triggered by cues, that lasting change comes not from willpower but from redesigning these loops, and that small keystone habits can reshape an entire life. This confirms what the monastic tradition knew, that we are formed by what we repeatedly do, and that a rule of life works because it installs the practices of discipleship below the level of constant decision.
secular.testedAgainstScripture: Habit science explains the mechanism of formation and is silent on its source and its goal. It can install a practice and cannot give the practice its power, which Scripture locates in the Spirit working through the means, not in the loop itself. A man can build the habit of reading the Bible and meet only ink, because the same disciplines that are channels of grace for an abiding heart are dead works for a self-powered one. The science rightly recovers the role of repeated practice. Only the gospel makes the practice a place of encounter rather than a treadmill.

secular.source: Peak and the science of expertise
secular.author: Anders Ericsson
secular.whatItGetsRight: Ericsson's research on how people reach mastery overturned the myth of natural talent, showing that expertise comes through deliberate practice, years of focused, effortful work at the edge of one's ability, guided by a teacher and aimed at specific weaknesses. This is the apprenticeship model the New Testament assumes, the long, attentive, guided practice by which a learner slowly becomes like a master, and it dignifies the unglamorous repetition that real growth requires.
secular.testedAgainstScripture: The research illuminates the how of becoming like Christ and cannot supply the relationship at its center. Deliberate practice produces an expert through the learner's own effort, but no amount of effort produces Christlikeness, which Scripture says is the fruit of the Spirit and not the achievement of the will. The disciple practices, yes, with all the focus Ericsson describes, but he practices in dependence, abiding in the vine rather than mastering a skill, receiving a life he cannot generate. The model rightly honors effortful apprenticeship. It mistakes who is finally doing the forming.

secular.source: Connected and the science of social contagion
secular.author: Nicholas Christakis and James Fowler
secular.whatItGetsRight: Christakis and Fowler showed with striking data that behaviors, habits, and even emotions spread through social networks, that we become like the people we are surrounded by, often without noticing, and that the company we keep shapes us more powerfully than our intentions do. This is Proverbs confirmed by network science, whoever walks with the wise becomes wise, and it explains why discipleship has always happened in community and why isolated Christians stall.
secular.testedAgainstScripture: The science confirms that we are formed by our communities and cannot tell us which community or to what end. Social contagion spreads vice as readily as virtue, and a person shaped only by their network is a leaf carried by whatever crowd they fell into. Scripture calls the disciple into a particular community, the body of Christ, formed around a particular person, and it warns that the companion of fools suffers harm. The research rightly recovers the power of community. The gospel tells us which body to be joined to and whose life is meant to spread through it.

secular.author: Alasdair MacIntyre and the Aristotelian tradition
secular.whatItGetsRight: MacIntyre and the virtue tradition recovered the ancient insight that a good life is not chiefly a matter of following rules but of becoming a certain kind of person, that virtues are formed by practice within a community and a tradition that gives them meaning, and that character is the slow product of habituation. This is a powerful corrective to a modern ethics of mere rule-keeping and choice, and it maps closely onto the biblical vision of a disciple being formed in the virtues of Christ.
secular.testedAgainstScripture: Virtue ethics rightly aims at character over rules and stops short of the one thing that makes Christian virtue possible, the new birth and the indwelling Spirit. Aristotle could describe the virtuous person and could not produce one in a sinner, because habituation can refine a nature but cannot replace it, and the human heart needs replacing. Scripture agrees that character is formed by practice in community, and it insists the community is the church, the tradition is the gospel, and the power is grace. The tradition rightly recovers the goal of a transformed person. Only Christ supplies the transformation that mere practice cannot reach.

secular.author: The modern self-help industry
secular.whatItGetsRight: The vast self-help literature is, at its best, a sincere attempt to answer the discipleship question the church often neglects, how do I actually become a better, freer, less anxious, more disciplined person. It has gathered real insight about goals, habits, attention, and the management of the inner life, and it testifies to a universal human hunger to be changed that the gospel alone finally answers.
secular.testedAgainstScripture: Self-help is discipleship with the master removed, a project of the self, by the self, for the sake of the self, and that is precisely its limit and its danger. Scripture says the self is the problem, not the savior, that the very ego doing the improving is the thing that must die, and that the goal is not a better me but a self crucified with Christ and raised to live for God. The self cannot lift itself, and a lifetime of trying only produces a more polished version of the old idolatry. The industry rightly names the hunger to be changed. It hands the hungry a mirror when they need a vine.

parts.title: Where Faithful Christians Differ
parts.body: Christians who long equally for real transformation still differ on where the weight of discipleship should fall, and the disagreement is between two emphases that each guard against a real distortion they have watched do damage. The dividing question is whether a believer is changed chiefly by practicing the spiritual disciplines or chiefly by deepening their grasp of the gospel of grace. Hear each view at its strongest, because the wisest disciples hold both and the argument is mostly about which one to lead with.

views.view: Lead with the disciplines: we are changed by practice
views.body: This view holds that transformation comes through the intentional practice of the spiritual disciplines, the ordinary means by which a person places themselves before God to be changed, prayer, fasting, solitude, silence, study, worship, confession, service. It takes seriously that we are embodied creatures formed by what we repeatedly do, and that no one drifts into Christlikeness any more than they drift into fluency or fitness. Advocates argue that the modern church has produced stalled believers precisely because it preached grace while neglecting the practices through which grace forms a life, leaving people waiting passively for a change that God means to work through their active participation. They point to Paul, who told Timothy to train himself for godliness the way an athlete trains his body, and to the whole monastic and Puritan tradition that built rules of life on purpose. The distortion they are guarding against is real, a cheap grace that talks endlessly about being accepted and produces no actual disciples, a Christianity so afraid of works that it has abandoned the means of growth. They are quick to add that the disciplines do not earn anything, that they are not the cause of change but the place we go to receive it, the way the branch does not strain to make fruit but stays where the life can reach it. Their aim is not effort against grace but effort that takes grace seriously enough to show up for it.

views.view: Lead with the gospel: we are changed by grasping grace
views.body: This view holds that transformation comes chiefly through an ever-deepening grasp of the gospel, that we are changed not by trying harder but by beholding more, as the glory of what God has done for us in Christ reorders the heart's loves from the inside out. It takes seriously that behavior flows from worship, that we become like what we treasure, and that the root of every sin is a failure to believe the gospel deeply enough in that moment. Advocates argue that disciplines pursued apart from a heart captured by grace produce either pride or despair, the Pharisee who succeeds and looks down, or the exhausted striver who fails and gives up, and that the engine of real change is not the will but a heart melted and remade by the love of God. They point to Paul, who said we are transformed by beholding the glory of the Lord, and to the whole gospel logic that puts the indicative of what God has done before the imperative of what we must do. The distortion they are guarding against is real, a joyless moralism that turns discipleship into a self-improvement project, that produces disciplined people who are subtly trusting their disciplines and have never been undone by grace. They are quick to add that grasping the gospel is not passive, that it requires the disciplines as the means of beholding, and that a faith which never moves into practice was never the gospel grasp it claimed. Their aim is not contemplation against effort but an effort that flows from a heart first captured by love.

parts.title: What Discipleship Forms in You
parts.body:
The goal of the whole apprenticeship is stated plainly and it is staggering, that we would be conformed to the image of God's Son. Not improved. Not made religious. Conformed to Christ, until his character becomes ours, until we love what he loves and are free the way he is free. Everything else discipleship forms is a facet of this one thing, the slow remaking of a person into the likeness of the one they follow, and it is the inheritance the stalled believer has been leaving in the box.

It forms the fruit of the Spirit, which is not a list of behaviors to perform but a character that grows. Love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness, self-control, these are what a branch produces when it stays in the vine over years, not what a striver manufactures in a weekend. The disciple does not work these up. They grow up in him, slowly and from the inside, as the life of Christ works its way into the deep places, and the surest sign that real discipleship is happening is not more activity but more of this fruit appearing where it was not before.

It forms an unhurried and unanxious life, because the disciple is learning to live from a source outside their own frantic effort. Jesus was the least hurried person who ever lived, never running, never frantic, fully present to the person in front of him, and to apprentice to him is to slowly catch his unhurriedness, to be cured of the driven anxiety that mistakes activity for life. The disciple is being set free from the need to prove, to perform, to hold the world together, because they are learning in their bones that they are held.

And it forms a love that spends itself, because you become like the one you follow, and the one we follow washed feet and went to a cross. The longer a person truly apprentices to Jesus, the more they find their life bending outward, toward the poor, the difficult, the enemy, the next person God puts in their path, not as a duty grimly performed but as the natural shape of a heart being remade in his image. That is the end of the long apprenticeship, a person who has become, in actual fact, a little more like Jesus, and there is no greater thing a human life can become, and no other thing the church was finally sent to make.

parts.title: Practice
parts.body: Discipleship is not admired into existence any more than wisdom is. It is the slow fruit of staying near the vine through ordinary practices sustained over years, in the company of others walking the same way. None of what follows will transform you by next month. All of it will start to form you if you keep at it, not because the practices have power in themselves but because they are where you go to receive the One who does. Begin with one thing, this week.

steps: Spend ten unhurried minutes a day simply being with Jesus before you do anything for him, with an open Bible and an open heart, not to study or to produce but to abide. The being with comes first, and most stalled believers have never simply sat with him.

Name the one sin you keep confessing and have never left, and instead of gritting your teeth at the behavior, ask what you are loving or fearing underneath it. Bring that root to Christ. Change comes at the level of worship, not willpower.

Tell one trusted believer the truth about where you actually are, saved and stuck, and ask them to walk with you. Discipleship has never been a solo project, and the first step out of the plateau is almost always confessing it to someone.

Do one small hidden act of service no one will see, for someone who cannot repay you. You become like the one you follow by doing the kinds of things he did, and the apprenticeship is learned in the doing, not only the studying.

Build the smallest sustainable rule of life, two or three practices you will actually keep, a fixed time with God, a weekly day of rest, a regular table with other believers. You are formed by what you repeatedly do, so design the repetitions on purpose.

Pick one spiritual discipline you have neglected, fasting, solitude, silence, generosity, and practice it once this month, not to earn anything but to put yourself where grace can reach a part of you that words have not.

Find a Wesley-style band of two or three who will meet to ask how it is with your soul, to confess honestly, and to watch over one another in love. The revival dies without the vessel, and the vessel is a small group of people telling each other the truth.

Read one of the Gospels slowly, watching not only what Jesus taught but how he lived, how he handled interruption, rest, anger, money, and the difficult person, and let the watching begin to reshape your instincts. You are apprenticing to a way of life, not only a set of beliefs.

Submit to a teacher and a tradition rather than discipling yourself, since the self cannot finally form the self. Find an older believer, a mentor, a wise community, and place yourself under their guidance the way an apprentice places himself under a master.

Let the disciplines move outward into mission, because a discipleship that only feeds the self has misunderstood the master. Take up one sustained service to the poor or the lost, and let it become a place where Christ forms you as you give yourself away.

Conduct an honest examen over the season. Where is the fruit of the Spirit appearing that was not there a year ago, and where is the same old hardness still ruling. Name both, thank God for the growth, and bring the hardness back to the vine.

Make one structural change that protects the apprenticeship from the tyranny of the urgent, since a busy life will crowd out discipleship by default. Guard the time with God the way you guard a meeting you cannot miss, because it is the most important appointment you keep.

Commit to a way of life for the long haul, since transformation is the work of years and not months, and the disciples who are changed are simply the ones who did not quit. Settle in for a long apprenticeship and stop expecting a shortcut.

Become a maker of disciples, not only a disciple, because the commission is to reproduce, and you learn the life most deeply by helping someone else learn it. Take one younger believer under your wing and walk with them the way someone walked with you.

Build your life around the means of grace as a permanent rhythm, the Word, the table, the gathered church, prayer, confession, generosity, so that abiding is not an effort you sustain but a structure that sustains you, the trellis on which a long life of fruit can grow.

Keep your eyes on the goal through every dry season, that you would be conformed to the image of the Son. The aim is not a busier Christian life or a more disciplined one, but a person who has become, over a lifetime of following, unmistakably like Jesus, and there is nothing else worth giving your one life to become.
